strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: reliable few-shot adaptation of smaller multimodal models. Adapting approximately 24M parameters while freezing the vision encoder and language model is a practical design.

The same-backbone comparisons provide useful evidence for meta-learning. In Table 1, MAPD improves average accuracy over Multi-TaskPD on all four datasets: 77.9 versus 74.6 on Open-MI, 47.7 versus 45.1 on Operator Induction, 31.4 versus 29.9 on CLEVR, and 26.4 versus 22.9 on TextOCR.

The experiments include prompt-length analysis, support-example selection, image perturbations, and larger-shot evaluations. The appendix provides substantial implementation detail and explicitly acknowledges the additional test-time computation.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited. MAPD combines established first-order MAML, learned visual prompt tokens, and an attention mapper explicitly inspired by prior work. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish its algorithmic contribution from existing meta-learned vision-language bridges and meta-prompt initialization methods, or compare directly against adapted versions of these approaches.

The central explanation—that irrelevant image embeddings cause ICL failures and task-specific distillation resolves them—is not isolated experimentally. All internal baselines share the attention mapper, while external comparisons change the backbone, training data, and adaptation procedure. Matched comparisons with an MLP projector, conventional prompt tuning or LoRA, and token compression without meta-learning are needed to establish which components produce the gains.

The evaluation is small and lacks uncertainty estimates. Operator Induction has only 60 query examples, and the other datasets have 200 each. No repeated-seed results, confidence intervals, or support-sampling variability are reported, making modest improvements over the strongest baselines difficult to assess.

The few-shot supervision budget needs qualification. Appendix A.2.2 reserves an additional 10% of each target dataset's training split for validation and selects an adaptation checkpoint for each support set using validation loss. Thus, adaptation depends on target-domain labels beyond the advertised shots. The construction of this validation set and its compatibility with episode-specific labels or hidden operations are insufficiently explained; results with a globally fixed adaptation schedule would strengthen the comparison.

Several claims exceed the evidence. Strictly monotonic improvement is contradicted by Appendix Table 7, where MAPD falls from 40.5 at eight shots to 40.0 at sixteen shots, and Table 8 shows a plateau. Table 9 also shows that LLaVA-OneVision-7B exceeds MAPD on CLEVR and TextOCR, so superiority over ICL is not general across the evaluated models and tasks.

The mathematical-reasoning analysis changes the supervision by adding manually written rationales and relies on an unvalidated model judge. Figure 15 contains an inconsistent original answer and the incorrect equation '5−1=−4'. Moreover, the scoring scheme awards one point when both reasoning and answer are wrong, so the reported 91.5% normalized score is not reasoning accuracy. These issues weaken the claimed reasoning improvement.

Efficiency comparisons are incomplete: MAPD uses approximately five times the test-time computation of ICL and substantially more training time than Multi-TaskPD, without compute-matched baselines. The narrow evaluation on four tasks and one proposed backbone does not yet establish benefits broad enough to compensate for the limited novelty and unresolved evaluation issues.

strengths: Addresses a relevant problem: improving few-shot adaptation of smaller multimodal models while keeping the vision encoder and language model frozen and training approximately 24M parameters.

The shared-architecture comparisons provide positive evidence for MAPD. In Table 1, its average accuracy exceeds Multi-TaskPD on all four datasets: 77.9 versus 74.6 on Open-MI, 47.7 versus 45.1 on Operator Induction, 31.4 versus 29.9 on CLEVR, and 26.4 versus 22.9 on TextOCR.

Includes useful analyses of prompt length, support-example selection, image perturbations, and adaptation steps. The paper also explicitly acknowledges the substantial test-time computational overhead.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited. MAPD combines an attention mapper inspired by Najdenkoska et al. with established first-order MAML and learned inner-loop learning rates. The paper does not clearly establish the advance beyond existing multimodal meta-learning and meta-prompt initialization approaches, or directly compare against those closest predecessors. The term 'distillation' describes feature compression without a distinct teacher-student objective.

The few-shot evaluation uses additional labeled target-domain data for model selection. Appendix A.2.2 reserves 10% of each evaluation dataset's training split and selects the lowest-validation-loss checkpoint for each adapted episode, as well as tuning learning rates. This is not test-set leakage, but it exceeds the advertised support-shot supervision budget and makes comparison with ICL less direct. Results with adaptation hyperparameters fixed on separate development tasks are needed.

Statistical support is insufficient for the relatively modest improvements over Multi-TaskPD. Evaluation uses only 60 Operator Induction queries and 200 queries for each other dataset, without confidence intervals or reported variability across training seeds and support-set resampling. Several differences could plausibly reflect sampling variation.

The experiments do not isolate the proposed explanation that irrelevant image information causes ICL failure. All principal baselines share the attention mapper, and the prompt-length study changes both training and adaptation strategy. Missing controls include a comparable MLP connector, alternative visual-token compression, and standard parameter-efficient adaptation under matched data and compute. MAPD also receives substantially more training computation than Multi-TaskPD.

Claims of consistent superiority and strictly monotonic scaling are overstated. Table 9 shows MAPD trailing LLaVA-OneVision-7B ICL on CLEVR and TextOCR, including 26.4 versus 42.3 on TextOCR. Table 8 shows its TextOCR accuracy plateauing at 31.5 from 32 to 64 shots, while Multi-TaskPD reaches 33.5. These findings support a narrower claim than the abstract and conclusion make.

The mathematical-reasoning analysis changes the supervision by adding hand-written rationales that explicitly name the hidden operation. Its judge-based score also assigns partial credit when both reasoning and answer are wrong, so it is not reasoning accuracy. No human calibration is reported, and Figure 15 contains an inconsistent example with an original answer of 10, a rewritten answer of 4, and the incorrect equation 5−1=−4. This weakens confidence in the auxiliary reasoning evidence.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite useful implementation details. The promised code link is absent, support-sampling repetitions and random seeds are unspecified, and the adaptation budget is described inconsistently as 30 steps per support set versus 30 steps per shot. Overall, the incremental contribution and unresolved evaluation limitations do not establish competitiveness for a top-tier conference.

strengths: Addresses a relevant problem: improving few-shot adaptation of smaller multimodal models while freezing the vision encoder and language model and training approximately 24M parameters.

The matched-architecture comparisons provide useful evidence for meta-learning. In Table 1, MAPD improves average accuracy over Multi-TaskPD on all four datasets, including 77.9 versus 74.6 on Open-MI and 47.7 versus 45.1 on Operator Induction.
Includes informative analyses of prompt length, support-example selection, image perturbations, and adaptation steps. Table 2 shows smaller accuracy drops under support-image perturbations.
The appendix provides substantial implementation detail, and the paper acknowledges the additional test-time computational cost.
weaknesses: The few-shot evaluation uses additional labeled target-dataset data. Appendix A.2.2 reserves 10% of each target training split for validation and selects an adaptation checkpoint for each support set using validation loss. These labels exceed the advertised shot budget and are not equivalently available to ordinary ICL. Results with a fixed adaptation schedule selected on separate development tasks are needed.

Statistical support is inadequate for the central gains: the evaluation contains only 60 Operator Induction queries and 200 queries per other dataset, with no reported confidence intervals or variation across training seeds and support sampling. Several improvements over strong matched baselines are small, such as 31.4 versus 30.9 on CLEVR.

The methodological novelty is limited and insufficiently distinguished from cited work on meta-learned vision-language bridges and meta-initialized prompt tuning. The method primarily combines an attention mapper with established first-order MAML. There are no controlled comparisons against ordinary projector adaptation, LoRA, or closely related published meta-prompt methods.

The proposed explanation involving irrelevant image-token information is not established experimentally. Comparing gradient adaptation with ICL changes the learning mechanism, supervision budget, and computation simultaneously; it does not isolate task-relevant feature distillation. Appendix A.4 reports approximately five times the test-time computation, without a compute-matched comparison.

Several claims exceed the evidence. Strictly monotonic improvement is contradicted by the TextOCR results in Table 8, which plateau at 31.5 from 32 to 64 shots. Table 9 also shows MAPD below LLaVA-OneVision-7B on CLEVR and TextOCR, limiting claims of consistently outperforming ICL.

The mathematical-reasoning analysis introduces hand-written reasoning supervision and an unvalidated model judge, so it does not cleanly diagnose the original task. Figure 15 contains an inconsistent example: the original answer is 10, the explanation concludes 4, and it states 5−1=−4. This raises concerns about the quality of the auxiliary supervision.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: reliable few-shot adaptation of smaller multimodal models. The frozen-backbone design and approximately 24M trainable connector parameters are practically appealing.

MAPD improves over the matched Multi-TaskPD baseline on all four datasets in Table 1, with gains of 3.3, 2.6, 1.5, and 3.5 percentage points. These comparisons provide concrete evidence that meta-training benefits adaptation.

The experimental analysis is extensive, including connector and prompt-length ablations, alternative backbones, image perturbations, support-example selection, higher-shot settings, and test-time computation. The appendix provides substantial implementation detail and acknowledges additional adaptation latency.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited relative to the acknowledged work on meta-learned multimodal prompts and attention mappers. The main ingredients are established first-order MAML, learned prompt tokens, and attention-based visual compression. A direct comparison with the closest prior approach, including a controlled CLS-token versus patch-feature ablation, is needed to establish the contribution beyond this combination.

The few-shot evaluation uses additional target-task supervision. Appendix A.2.3 reserves 10% of each target training split for validation and describes selecting the best adaptation checkpoint for each support set using that validation loss, alongside learning-rate selection. This is not test-query leakage, but it exceeds the advertised support-shot budget. The paper should distinguish global hyperparameter selection from per-episode checkpoint selection and report performance with a fixed adaptation schedule selected independently of target tasks.

The statistical evidence is insufficiently justified. Thousands of evaluation episodes reuse test pools containing only 60–200 examples, yet the paper reports very narrow binomial confidence intervals without explaining their construction or handling dependence across episodes and shot settings. For example, the CLEVR interval of ±0.2 percentage points is difficult to reconcile with the stated evaluation counts using a straightforward binomial calculation. Multiple training seeds and uncertainty estimates that respect the sampling structure are needed.

The headline gains do not isolate the contribution of meta-learning. The 7.7-point comparison with LoRA changes both adaptation parameterization and training strategy; the matched Multi-TaskPD comparison yields only about 2.7 points on average. MAPD also receives approximately 10 hours of training versus 4.5 hours for Multi-TaskPD. A compute-matched multitask baseline and meta-trained LoRA would make the attribution more convincing.

The proposed explanation for ICL failure remains speculative. Replacing images with text changes perceptual difficulty as well as token content, while replacing ICL with supervised adaptation changes the learning mechanism and computation. Neither comparison isolates irrelevant visual information. Furthermore, higher attention entropy does not establish better task-relevant processing, so the entropy analysis does not validate the claimed mechanism.

The scope and competitiveness claims exceed the evidence. Cross-backbone experiments cover only Open-MI, and Table 13 shows stronger public-model baselines: connector-finetuned LLaVA-OneVision-7B exceeds MAPD on three of four datasets, including Open-MI, contradicting the appendix's state-of-the-art Open-MI claim. The results support improvement within the proposed architecture, but do not establish broad superiority or applicability to arbitrary LMMs.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: improving few-shot adaptation in multimodal models while keeping the language model frozen and the visual prompt length fixed.
Controlled comparisons using the same backbone favor MAPD over Multi-TaskPD on all four dataset averages, with improvements of 3.3, 2.6, 1.5, and 3.5 percentage points in Table 1.

The evaluation includes substantial architectural ablations, alternative training objectives, LoRA comparisons, support-image perturbations, and additional backbone configurations. The appendix also acknowledges adaptation latency and provides a compute comparison.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited. MAPD combines established first-order MAML, learned prompts, and an attention mapper explicitly inspired by prior work. The paper does not sufficiently establish its advance over existing meta-learned visual prompting beyond using patch features and applying the combination to LMMs.

The few-shot evaluation uses additional labeled target-dataset validation examples. Appendix A.2.3 selects an adaptation checkpoint for each support set using this validation set, which also determines learning rates. This is not test-query leakage, but it introduces supervision beyond the advertised shots and complicates comparison with ICL. Results with adaptation settings fixed on separate development tasks are needed.

Statistical reporting is insufficiently justified. Thousands of episodes reuse only 60–200 underlying query examples per dataset, yet the paper reports very narrow binomial confidence intervals without explaining dependence, aggregation across shots, or training-seed variability. This limits confidence in the relatively small gains over Multi-TaskPD.

The headline improvements do not isolate meta-learning's contribution. The 21.2-point gain compares MAPD with ICL, while the 7.7-point gain compares against non-meta-trained LoRA. The closest training-objective comparison, Multi-TaskPD, yields about 2.7 points on average. MAPD also receives approximately 10 training hours versus 4.5 for Multi-TaskPD; a compute-matched control and meta-trained LoRA would strengthen attribution.

The proposed explanation involving irrelevant image embeddings remains speculative. Text-versus-image comparisons conflate perception and representation difficulty, and reduced attention entropy does not establish that a model cannot use relevant tokens. The mathematical-reasoning analysis additionally changes support supervision by supplying hand-written rationales, so it does not cleanly decompose performance on the original task.

Broad generalization and state-of-the-art claims exceed the evidence. Evaluation covers four narrow tasks, and alternative-backbone experiments cover only Open-MI. Table 13 reports stronger results from existing models, including fine-tuned LLaVA-OneVision-7B on three of four tasks. Claims of monotonic improvement also do not extend to the higher-shot TextOCR results in Table 18.

Reproducibility and reporting need correction: the promised code link is blank, main-table captions describe averaging over five shot counts while Table 11 uses four per dataset, and the confidence-interval computation is unspecified. These issues matter because the acceptance case depends primarily on empirical evidence.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: reliable few-shot adaptation of smaller multimodal models when in-context learning saturates or deteriorates. Adapting a compact visual connector while freezing the backbone is a practical approach.
The controlled comparison in Table 1 is encouraging. MAPD outperforms the same-architecture Multi-TaskPD baseline on all four dataset averages, with gains of 3.3, 2.6, 1.5, and 3.5 percentage points.

The experimental coverage includes connector and prompt ablations, several backbone configurations, support-image perturbations, example-selection strategies, and test-time compute analysis. Reporting the additional adaptation latency is useful.
The appendix supplies substantial implementation information, including training mixtures, hyperparameter searches, task construction, and per-shot results.
weaknesses: The few-shot evaluation uses additional labeled target-task data for model selection. Appendix A.2.3 reserves 10% of each evaluation dataset's training split and selects the adaptation checkpoint separately after processing each support set. Thus, the reported results are not based solely on the advertised few-shot supervision. The relationship between this validation pool and episode-specific label mappings or operators is insufficiently explained. A fixed adaptation schedule selected on separate development tasks is needed to establish the central low-data claim.

The uncertainty estimates are insufficiently justified. Table 9 lists only 60–200 test examples per dataset, whereas Table 5 constructs thousands of episodes that necessarily reuse queries. The reported binomial intervals do not explain how query reuse, support sampling, and averaging across shot settings are handled; some intervals are unexpectedly narrow even relative to the stated episode counts. Multiple training seeds and uncertainty estimates accounting for shared queries are needed, particularly because the incremental gains over Multi-TaskPD are modest.

The methodological novelty is limited relative to the acknowledged prior work on meta-learning visual-language bridges and soft prompts. The main ingredients are an attention mapper, patch features, and established first-order MAML. A direct comparison with Najdenkoska et al. (2023), including its CLS-based mapper under matched conditions, would better establish the contribution beyond applying existing ideas to larger models.

The comparisons do not fully isolate the benefit of meta-learning. MAPD receives repeated inner-loop training and approximately 10 hours of finetuning, versus 4.5 hours for Multi-TaskPD. There is no training-compute-matched multitask control or meta-trained LoRA baseline. Consequently, the reported 7.7-point advantage over LoRA cannot be attributed specifically to meta-learning.

The broad state-of-the-art and architectural generality claims exceed the evidence. Table 13 shows that ordinary connector finetuning of LLaVA-OneVision-7B exceeds MAPD on three of four datasets, while Qwen2.5-VL-7B exceeds it on three as well. These comparisons have training-data confounds, but still contradict an unqualified state-of-the-art claim. Backbone variation is evaluated only on Open-MI, and replacing components within one framework does not demonstrate integration into arbitrary LMM architectures.

The proposed mechanism remains a hypothesis. Textualizing images removes perceptual difficulty as well as irrelevant visual information, and finetuning changes the learning procedure and compute budget. Neither comparison isolates visual distraction. Likewise, more uniform attention does not establish better task-relevant feature extraction. The evidence supports empirical adaptation gains more strongly than the claimed explanation.
